In the last video, you learned how to find and define requirements
that describe what your application should and shouldn't do.

But to find out whether your application meets those requirements,
you need to run it through those situations that test them.

So in this video, you'll learn how to come up with those situations
and turn them into test cases,

specifying what you'll give the application and what
you expect it to do.

Each test case should keep together the user request,
the relevant records or context, and the expected outcome.

This can be tricky because a single requirement can apply in lots of
different situations,
so you'll want an initial set of cases that covers a meaningful range.

For example, the shelter application must only match volunteers with
dogs they can safely handle.

That includes volunteers with different levels of experience,
dogs with different handling needs,
and situations where information about either one of those is missing.

One case won't tell you whether the application follows the rule
across those different situations.

So, let's start choosing situations for that safe
matching requirement.

A volunteer needs the experience and physical ability to handle the
dog safely, and you'll want cases that test both.

Otherwise, you could have lots of cases about experience without ever
checking whether the volunteer can physically control the dog.

You can get those situations from a few different angles.
One approach is to think about what would make a match safe or unsafe.

For a dog that needs an experienced handler,
you could consider a first-time volunteer,

and then someone with the experience and physical ability to
handle that dog safely.

You could also consider an experienced volunteer who can't
physically control the dog.

These situations let you check whether the application considers both
experience and physical ability when making a match.

Another approach is to consider what information the application will
have about the volunteer or dog.

You might try a situation with clear handling notes,
one where those notes are missing,

and one where two notes disagree about whether a
beginner can handle the dog.

That lets you test what the application does when the information it
has is incomplete or contradictory.

A third approach is to change how the request is written while keeping
the facts the same. For example, "Can I take Buddy out for a walk?"

and "I'd like to walk Buddy. Would that be okay?" ask for the same
thing. And you can also try shorter messages or spelling mistakes.

You're checking whether the application makes the same decision
when someone asks in a different way.

These are ways to get ideas, so you don't have to apply all three to
every case or try every possible combination.

Start with situations the application is likely to face and problems
you've already seen,
especially where a mistake could put someone at risk.

Once you've chosen some situations to test your requirement,
the next step is to work out what goes into each test case.

For the shelter, you'll need the volunteer request, the volunteer
and dog information, and what you expect the agent to do.

them to control safely.

and availability conditions are met,
and the shelter's policy calls for approving suitable matches.

But if the dog's handling notes are missing,
should the agent ask for more information or reject the match?
The safe matching requirement doesn't settle that question.

Check the shelter's policy, and if it doesn't answer the question,
ask the people responsible to decide.

If the decision is to ask for the missing information
before recommending a match,
add that to the requirement and write it down as the expected outcome.

Until that decision is made, you don't yet know what response
to count as correct.
